title: Elevator Scheduling Algorithms
description: Compare SCAN, LOOK, and shortest-seek-time-first for multi-elevator coordination.

data.text: Your building has 4 elevators. Peak hours create bursts of requests. Choose and implement a scheduling algorithm that minimizes average wait time.
Different scheduling algorithms trade fairness against efficiency. LOOK is common in real systems because it avoids unnecessary travel to the end of the shaft.

data.title: Scheduling Algorithms
items: **FCFS**: First Come First Served. Fair but slow during bursts.
**SSTF**: Shortest Seek Time First. Fast per request but can starve distant floors.
**SCAN**: Elevator sweeps all floors in one direction, then reverses. Predictable but visits empty floors.
**LOOK**: Like SCAN but reverses at the last requested floor, not the physical end. Best real-world choice.
**Weighted**: Weight requests by wait time to prevent starvation.

data.title: Elevator Scheduler Interface
Why LOOK over SCAN?
data.text: SCAN always goes to floor 1 or the top floor even if no one is waiting there. LOOK reverses at the last requested floor, saving time and energy. Most modern elevator controllers use LOOK or variants.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: LOOK minimizes travel distance while preserving fairness
Prefer elevators already moving toward the request
Idle elevators should move toward the nearest waiting request
Always have a fallback when all elevators are busy
data.takeaway: Elevator scheduling is a microcosm of load balancing: combine proximity, direction, and queue depth to pick the best resource.
